56-013.r: Largest groundnut producer 2020-21 → Gujarat; in 2024-25: Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh.

56-014.r: Largest groundnut producer → Gujarat (when asked and in 2024-25), followed by Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh.

56-015.r: Low acreage but very high groundnut yield (when asked) → Punjab; top yields in 2024-25: West Bengal, Gujarat, Tamil Nadu.

56-016.r: Odd one out: Groundnut (pods form underground) or Castor seed (oil not used as food); sesame, groundnut and mustard oils are edible.
56-016.c: The book gives no single answer (*): groundnut is odd by where it forms, castor by its inedible oil. Groundnut pods grow underground from the flower's peg, not from the root.

56-017.r: Rajasthan → chief producer of rapeseed and mustard (also in 2024-25).

56-018.r: Map A-D: Gujarat → Groundnut; Maharashtra → Sugarcane (and cotton); Odisha → Ragi; Andhra Pradesh → Tobacco.

56-019.r: Oilseeds when asked (descending): Soybean, Groundnut, Mustard, Sesamum. 2024-25 (Mt): Soyabean 15.27, Mustard 12.67, Groundnut 11.94, Sesamum 0.83.

56-020.r: Varuna, Pusa Bold, Jaikisan → Mustard varieties.

56-022.r: Pitambari → yellow mustard variety; matures in 110-115 days; average yield 1536 kg per hectare.

56-023.r: Large quantity of gypsum → needed for Groundnut cultivation.

56-024.r: Kaushal → groundnut variety (also Chitra-64, Chandra). Gram: Pant-114, Gaurav, Radhe; Cotton: Suvin, Sujata; Wheat: Kundan, Kalyan Sona, Sonalika.

56-025.r: Highest oil content → Sesame 52%; Groundnut 48.2%, Sunflower 42%, Soyabean 40%.

56-026.r: Safflower → Carthamus tinctorius; seeds 24-36% oil, rich in linoleic acid (78%); major states Maharashtra and Karnataka.

57-001.r: Only statement 1 true: Black gram (urad) can be kharif and rabi crop (both in South India). Green gram is far below half of pulse output.

57-002.r: Major producer and consumer of pulses → India (largest producer in 2022, then Canada, China).

57-003.r: Not usually exported → Pulses (India imports them despite big output, due to high consumption); wheat, rice, sugar are exported at times.

57-004.r: India → largest producer, consumer and importer of pulses (2022): gram (chana), lentil (masoor), pigeon pea (arhar/toor).

57-005.r: India: shortage of pulses but not of protein sources (A true); high demand for pulses (R true); book: R explains A.

57-006.r: Largest pulses producer → Madhya Pradesh (when asked and in 2024-25).

57-007.r: Crops that fix nitrogen from the air → Legumes (with special bacteria), so they need less nitrogen fertilizer.

57-008.r: Nutrient essential for pulse crops → Cobalt (needed for Rhizobium's symbiotic nitrogen fixation; also vitamin B synthesis).

57-009.r: Wrong pair: Arhar — Neelam; Neelam is a mango variety. Correct: Groundnut → Chandra; Lentil → Pant L-406; Mustard → Varuna.

57-010.r: Gram, pea and moong fix atmospheric nitrogen; Rajma (kidney bean) fixes some, but its capacity varies.
57-010.c: The book gives no single answer (*): Rajma does fix some nitrogen, so no option is fully right; the intended answer is likely Rajma.

57-011.r: Balanced NPK ratio for legume crops → 1:2:2 (legumes may need 0:1:1, 1:2:2 or 1:2:3).
57-011.h: Legumes make their own nitrogen, so N gets the smallest share.

57-013.r: Malaviya Chamatkar → Arhar (pigeon pea) variety; other Arhar varieties: Bahar, Amar, Azad, Malaviya Vikas, Paras.

57-017.r: Largest pulses producer in 2011-12 → Madhya Pradesh (still first in 2024-25).

57-018.r: Wrong pair: Linseed — Surya; Surya is a mango, papaya and potato variety. Correct: Mustard → Varuna; Field pea → Sapna; Groundnut → Kaushal.

58-001.r: Largest silk producer → Karnataka: 44.15% of mulberry silk and 41.69% of raw silk (2023-24).

58-002.r: Over three-fourths of raw silk (when asked) → Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh; now (2023-24) over 58.99%. Leading mulberry silk state → Karnataka.

58-004.r: Silk leaders (2023-24): Mulberry → Karnataka (44.15%); Tasar → Jharkhand (71.06%); Eri → Assam (56.56%); Muga → Assam (65.6%).
58-004.h: Assam holds Eri and Muga; Jharkhand Tasar; Karnataka Mulberry.

58-006.r: Muga silk (one of the rarest) → Assam (65.6%), then Meghalaya (16.67%), 2023-24.

58-007.r: Oak Tasar silk (oak flora found 1966) → Manipur; tropical tasar → Jharkhand, the leading tasar state.

58-008.r: Largest producer of silk textiles/garments → Karnataka.

58-009.r: Maximum silk yarn → Karnataka (2023-24). India alone produces all five silks: Mulberry, Eri, Muga, Tropical Tasar, Temperate Tasar.

59-001.r: National Horticulture Board → set up 1984 as a society (Society Registration Act of 1860); headquarters Gurugram, Haryana.

59-002.r: Coffee → hot, humid tropical climate, propagated by seeds; tea → tropical and subtropical, propagated by stem cuttings → both true.

59-003.r: Largest coffee producer → Karnataka 70.43%; Kerala 20.07%, Tamil Nadu 5.30% (2024-25). Main varieties: Arabica and Robusta.

59-006.r: Karnataka alone → over 70% of India's coffee (70.43%, 256000 MT in 2024-25).

59-007.r: Largest area under coffee → Karnataka (2020-21), then Kerala, then Tamil Nadu.

59-008.r: Chikmagalur (Karnataka) → coffee (first grown in India here), not sugar; Mandya → sugar, not coffee → neither statement correct.
59-008.t: Swap trap: Chikmagalur = coffee, Mandya = sugar.

59-009.r: Not in Karnataka → Pulneys (hill range near Kodaikanal, Tamil Nadu); Chikmagalur, Coorg, Baba Budangiri are Karnataka coffee areas.

60-001.r: Tea states: major → Assam, West Bengal, Tamil Nadu, Kerala; small scale → Tripura, Himachal Pradesh and others; Andhra Pradesh not counted → three of four.

60-002.r: When asked, India led in production and consumption of both pulses and tea; FAO 2024: India second in tea leaves, still first in pulses.
60-002.c: The book gives no single answer (*): at the time both (b) tea and (d) pulses fitted; today only pulses.

60-003.r: Tea 2007-08 → India first in production and consumption; FAO 2024: China first, India second in tea leaf production.

60-004.r: Maximum foreign exchange among these cash crops → Tea exports; 2024-25 exports 257.88 million kg (Tea Board of India).

60-005.r: Largest tea producer → Assam (tops both area and production, 2024-25).

60-006.r: India produces more tea than it needs and exports it (257.88 million kg in 2024-25; third among exporters, FAO 2024); it imported cereals, petroleum, petro-chemicals.

60-007.r: India → major tea exporter (A true), but its domestic tea consumption is not poor (R false). Top exporters 2024: Kenya, China, India, Sri Lanka.

60-008.r: Tea → ideal on sloping hills with heavy rainfall (150-200 cm; question: over 200 cm).

60-010.r: Wrong pair: Coffee Board — Hyderabad; it is in Bengaluru. Correct: Spices Board → Kochi; Tea Board → Kolkata; Rubber Board → Kottayam.
60-010.h: Kerala hosts two boards: Spices (Kochi) and Rubber (Kottayam).

60-011.r: Barak Valley: main crop Rice, second Sugarcane → answer Sugarcane since rice is not an option.

60-012.r: Largest rubber producer → Kerala (Ernakulam, Kottayam, Kozhikode, Kollam); India 6th in natural rubber production (FAO 2024).
